issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly states that the methods and results were written using a randomized Qualtrics-generated dataset and will be updated after data collection. Nevertheless, the abstract and results present these simulated values as substantive empirical findings. This makes the current manuscript uninterpretable as evidence and prevents valid peer review of the actual study outcomes.
issues.quote:
[IMPORTANT: 
Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The abstract makes substantive conclusions about the effect of analytical reasoning and perceived impact even though the reported data are simulated/random. Such claims cannot be supported by dummy data and should not be presented as empirical results.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the “perceived impact of donation” as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The manuscript states both that results are based on randomized/dummy data to be updated later and that data collection was completed before analyses. These statements are incompatible and obscure whether the reported analyses are exploratory simulations, preregistration placeholders, or real data analyses.
issues.quote: All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.description: The methods state that participants selected their own intervention and identifiability conditions. This destroys random assignment, creates selection bias, and invalidates causal interpretation of differences between conditions. It also conflicts with the experimental framing and ANOVA-based causal tests.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The design is described as within-subject, but the tables and analyses show separate groups in six cells with sample sizes summing to N = 1000, implying a between-subject factorial design. If the design was truly within-subject, the analysis should model repeated measures; if it was between-subject, the description is wrong. This affects interpretation, degrees of freedom, standard errors, and validity of tests.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.subcategory: wrong analysis for stated within-subject design
issues.description: A standard 2 × 3 ANOVA with residual df = 994 is reported, which is consistent with a between-subject design, not the stated within-subject design. If participants experienced multiple conditions, a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed-effects model would be required; otherwise the design statement must be corrected.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: hypothetical donation instead of real donation
issues.description: The original dependent variable was actual donation of endowed money; the replication uses an imaginary donation. Hypothetical willingness to donate is not equivalent to actual prosocial behavior and may inflate or alter effects because there is no real cost. This is a major construct-validity threat to the claimed replication.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original study gave participants $5 before the donation decision. The replication removes the pre-survey/endowment procedure, changing the psychological meaning of the decision from allocating owned money to making a hypothetical rating. Endowment effects, loss aversion, and perceived ownership may materially affect donation behavior.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: Combining Studies 1 and 3 into one six-condition design changes the target experiments rather than directly replicating either. Applying the explicit intervention to the joint condition creates a condition not present in the original study and changes the meaning of the implicit manipulation. The merged design may introduce confounds and makes comparison to the original effects difficult.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect, indicated in the imaginary donation to corresponding victims across conditions. The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.description: The study is classified as a close to very close replication despite multiple consequential deviations: online MTurk setting, hypothetical donation, no real endowment, updated stimuli, added joint-intervention condition, and added measures. These are not merely minor deviations and limit the interpretability of the study as a close replication.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication |

issues.subcategory: intervention does not directly measure deliberative thinking
issues.description: The theoretical construct is deliberative or analytical thinking, but the manipulation is learning about the identifiable victim effect. Awareness of a bias, demand characteristics, experimenter demand, and explicit instruction are not equivalent to spontaneous deliberative reasoning. Without a manipulation check, it is unclear whether deliberative thought was actually induced.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.description: The manuscript describes joint presentation of identifiable and statistical victims as 'implicitly learning' about the identifiable victim effect. Joint evaluation may induce comparison, numeracy, or perceived scope, but it is not learning about the effect. This conflates different psychological mechanisms and weakens theoretical interpretation.
issues.quote: For Hypothesis 3 and 4, explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect means that participants would be presented with prior research about the phenomenon while participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.description: Teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect immediately before asking for donations may cue the desired response and induce demand compliance rather than analytical reasoning. The manuscript does not report a placebo control matched for reading time, educational content, or demand characteristics.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.description: The study’s central claim concerns deliberative/analytical thinking, but no measure is reported to verify that the intervention increased deliberation, reduced affective processing, or changed awareness as intended. Without manipulation checks, null or significant effects cannot be attributed to the proposed mechanism.
issues.quote: Our first goal is to conduct independent (close) replications of the identifiable victim effect, particularly on debiasing the identifiable victim effect through inducing a calculative thinking mechanism.

issues.subcategory: joint condition confounds identifiability with information amount
issues.description: The joint condition includes both identifiable information and statistics, so it differs from other conditions in amount, type, and complexity of information. Any effect could reflect information load, scope, comparison, salience, or target ambiguity rather than implicit deliberation or identifiability.
issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information.

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between Qualtrics-generated responses and MTurk recruitment, while key sample characteristics and compensation are unspecified. Without actual recruitment details, inclusion criteria, country restrictions, approval rates, and compensation, the sample cannot be evaluated or replicated.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: The replication sample is described as not specified for geographic origin and compensation. These are essential for evaluating comparability to the original sample, participant motivation, and generalizability.
issues.quote:
Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified
Gender | Not specified | 529 males, 471 females | 529 males, 471 females
Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The reported generated sample has a median age of 68 and an age range up to 120, which is highly atypical for MTurk and likely reflects dummy data. Any claims about human prosocial behavior or replication of a university-student laboratory sample cannot be generalized from such a sample without justification.
issues.quote:
Median age (years) | Not specified | 68 | 68
Average age (years) | Not specified | 67.8 | 67.8
Age range (years) | Not specified | 18-120 | 18-120

issues.description: The manuscript says participants with prior knowledge and failed attention checks were excluded, but does not report how many were excluded, whether exclusions occurred before or after condition assignment, or whether exclusions differed by condition. Differential exclusions can bias treatment effects and must be transparently reported.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: No procedure is provided for incomplete surveys, item nonresponse, partial missingness, duplicate responses, or attrition from the online survey. This is necessary to reproduce the analyses and evaluate possible bias.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The manuscript mentions excluding attention-check failures but does not provide the attention-check item, failure rule, timing, or whether it was preregistered. Attention checks can introduce post-treatment selection bias if placed after manipulations.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The manuscript states that data collection was launched at the start of the study period but does not clearly establish that preregistration occurred before any data collection or data inspection. Ambiguous timing weakens the evidentiary value of the preregistration.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.subcategory: power analysis not reported in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript says the sample size was determined by power analysis but provides no target effect, alpha, desired power, allocation ratio, planned exclusions, smallest effect of interest, or required per-cell sample size. Referring to a supplement is insufficient for evaluating whether the study is adequately powered for the interaction and extension hypotheses.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.subcategory: wrong target effect for replication evaluation
issues.description: The replication evaluation is described as comparing the effect of deliberative thinking to the original main effect of identifiability, d = 0.48. The central replication claim concerns the interaction between identifiability and deliberative intervention, not the main effect of identifiability. Using the wrong target effect can misclassify replication success.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84]) obtained from the power analysis using the criteria set by Lebel, Vanpaemel, Cheung, and Campbell (2019)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent original Study 1 degrees of freedom
issues.description: For a 2 × 2 between-subject ANOVA with N = 121, the residual df would ordinarily be 117, not 115. The manuscript reports df2 = 115 in Table 1, while later reporting a t-test with df = 117. This inconsistency suggests an error in extracting or reconstructing original statistics or unreported missing data.
issues.quote: Effect of identifiability and intervention on donation (Study 1) (N=121)

issues.description: The one-way ANOVA for original Study 3 reports df1 = 2 but leaves df2 as N/A despite N = 159; df2 should be reported to evaluate the F test and effect-size calculation. Omitting df prevents independent verification.
issues.quote: Effect of identifiability on donation (Study 3) (N=159)

issues.subcategory: condition labels reversed in results interpretation
issues.description: The text reverses the marginal means implied by Table 7. From the reported cell means, identifiable conditions average about 2.54 and statistical conditions average about 2.25, but the text states the opposite. This changes the substantive conclusion about whether the identifiable victim effect replicated.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.description: Table 7 shows higher donation in the identifiable condition than in the statistical condition when collapsed across intervention, but the narrative claims statistical victims received more. This internal inconsistency undermines trust in the reported analyses and conclusions.
issues.quote:
Table 7

Descriptive statistics for donation across conditions

Identifiable victim condition | Statistical victim condition | Joint condition
Intervention condition | 2.58 [1.77] (159) | 2.46 [1.69] (175) | 2.37 [1.62] (166)
No intervention condition | 2.50 [1.75] (175) | 2.01 [1.61] (159) | 2.67 [1.62] (166)

issues.subcategory: test statistic sign inconsistent with means
issues.description: The post-hoc test reports t = -2.40 for Identifiable vs Statistical while the descriptive means imply Identifiable > Statistical. Unless the contrast was coded in the reverse direction, the sign is inconsistent; the manuscript does not explain the contrast coding.

issues.subcategory: effect size inconsistent with mean difference
issues.description: The reported Cohen’s d values for pairwise comparisons appear too small relative to the reported mean differences and standard deviations. For example, an identifiable-statistical marginal difference of roughly 0.29 with SDs near 1.7 would imply d around 0.17, not 0.076. The calculation method is not described.
issues.quote: Identifiable VS Statistical | 994 | -2.40 | 0.13 | d | 0.076 | 95%CI | [-0.05, 0.20] | pBonferroni | .049*

issues.subcategory: significant p-value with confidence interval including zero
issues.description: Several pairwise comparisons are marked significant while the reported 95% confidence intervals for the effect size include zero. For the same contrast and confidence level, this is inconsistent unless the CI refers to a different estimand or is adjusted differently, which is not explained.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate or unjustified ANOVA for bounded donation variable
issues.description: Donation is constrained to six possible values from $0 to $5, making it bounded and likely ordinal/discrete. The original study used ordered probit as an additional analysis, but the replication drops it and relies on linear ANOVA without justifying distributional assumptions or robustness.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The donation outcome is bounded and discrete, and aggregated feelings are likely Likert-scale averages. Pearson correlations may be acceptable under some conditions, but the manuscript provides no justification, diagnostics, or robustness checks such as Spearman correlations or ordinal/linear models.
issues.quote: Correlation between aggregated feelings and donation | Linear Pearson’s correlation

issues.description: The manuscript tests many outcomes and effects: donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, perceived impact, multiple post-hoc tests, and six correlations. Except for selected Bonferroni pairwise tests, there is no familywise or false-discovery correction, increasing the risk that significant p = .045 findings are false positives.
issues.quote: We conducted a  2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions

issues.description: The analysis plan says post-hoc tests are conducted only if omnibus effects are significant. This creates data-dependent branching and does not specify all planned contrasts, alpha allocation, or simple-effect tests in advance. The approach is especially problematic with many hypotheses and outcomes.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test   (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: contrast does not match interaction hypothesis
issues.description: After a significant interaction, the manuscript compares the identifiable/no-intervention cell against the average of all other five conditions. This omnibus contrast does not directly test the predicted simple interaction that intervention reduces giving to identifiable victims but not statistical victims, and combining heterogeneous conditions can obscure or create effects.
issues.quote: we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of  identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.description: The manuscript aggregates conceptually different variables—being upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and possibly perceived impact—without reporting reliability, factor structure, scaling, or theoretical justification. Some items are emotions, while others are moral judgments or efficacy beliefs.
issues.quote: Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: perceived impact treated as affective feeling
issues.description: Perceived impact is an efficacy judgment, not an affective feeling. Treating it as one of the 'segregated affective reactions' or adding it to an affective scale confounds emotional and cognitive constructs.
issues.quote: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)

issues.subcategory: extension hypothesis contradicted by abstract conclusion
issues.description: The manuscript hypothesizes that identifiable victims elicit higher perceived impact, but the abstract says results supported lower perceived impact for identifiable or joint conditions. The direction of the extension is inconsistent across sections.
issues.quote: 6 (Extension) | An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims

issues.subcategory: results do not support stated perceived-impact hypothesis
issues.description: The reported significant post-hoc comparison is between statistical and joint conditions, not between identifiable and statistical victims. Therefore the results do not directly support Hypothesis 6 as stated.
issues.quote: Significant differences were found between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition, t(994)=2.47, SE=0.11, p=.041. This suggested that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=3.12, SD=1.43) had a higher rating of perceived impact of their donation to help the victims than they faced an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics (M=2.85, SD=1.34).

issues.description: The study uses simple correlations between feelings and donation but describes them as testing whether feelings predict donation. Because feelings and donations are measured in the same study without temporal precedence or experimental manipulation of feelings, predictive or causal interpretations are not warranted.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: causal language from nonrandom or unclear assignment
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly uses causal language such as 'effect' and 'reduces' even though assignment is described as participant-selected and the reported data are simulated. Without random assignment to conditions and real data, causal claims are not justified.
issues.quote: Learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces people’s donation tendency

issues.description: The manuscript says victim information will be updated from Save the Children but does not include the exact text, date accessed, victim characteristics, statistics, images, or equivalence checks. Updated stimuli can change identifiability, vividness, severity, credibility, and emotional impact.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.subcategory: online setting changes control over procedure
issues.description: Moving from a lab/student-center donation context to an online MTurk survey changes privacy, attention, social context, credibility, and perceived reality of the donation. The manuscript notes the change but does not add procedural controls or discuss how these differences may affect the psychological process.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: For MTurk/online data, the manuscript does not report eligibility restrictions, duplicate-prevention, bot detection, IP/location checks, device restrictions, minimum completion time, or approval criteria. These details are necessary for evaluating data quality.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: broad claims about humans and people
issues.description: The manuscript generalizes to 'humans' and 'people' despite relying on a specific online or generated sample and a particular charity context involving African victims. Cultural, age, platform, and donation-context limitations are not adequately acknowledged.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is the human’s tendency to offer greater support to an identifiable individual over a larger group of anonymous victims represented by numerical statistics

issues.subcategory: actual giving not generalizable from hypothetical response
issues.description: Because the replication asks for imaginary donations without real financial consequences, findings should be generalized only to stated intentions, not actual helping behavior. The discussion of donating behavior and prosocial motivation overreaches the operationalized outcome.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: questionnaire items and scale anchors absent
issues.description: The manuscript lists constructs but does not provide exact item wording, response scales, anchors, scoring, item order, or whether items were adapted from the original. These details are required to evaluate construct validity and enable replication.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation. These items included beliefs about the severity of the crisis, the perceived trustworthiness of the charity, the expected accountability of funds, evaluation of organizational efficiency, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.description: Essential methodological information is deferred to supplements and cloud folders, some of which contain placeholders. A manuscript should include enough details to evaluate the design and analyses without relying on incomplete external links.
issues.quote:
Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>
Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: Table 4 duplicated columns and sample size entries
issues.description: Table 4 appears to have duplicated replication columns and duplicated sample-size entries, making the sample comparison unclear. This is a reporting error that contributes to confusion about the actual sample.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.description: The manuscript involves human participants, deception or bias instruction, and charitable donation decisions, but it does not report ethics approval, informed consent, debriefing, or participant payment procedures. These are necessary for ethical and methodological evaluation.
issues.quote: Method

issues.subcategory: null effects interpreted without equivalence testing
issues.description: The manuscript treats nonsignificant results as 'no empirical support' or as evidence that effects are absent, but no equivalence tests, Bayes factors, smallest effect size of interest, or precision-based criteria are reported. A null p-value alone does not establish no effect.
issues.quote: found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: deviation from original analyses not justified
issues.description: The original analysis included ordered probit regression for the bounded donation outcome, but the replication omits it. The rationale for dropping this analysis is not provided, raising concerns about analytic flexibility and comparability to the target study.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's d values for main effects and an interaction from ANOVA results, including effects with more than two levels, but does not explain how d was computed or whether it is appropriate. Omnibus ANOVA effects are usually summarized with η²/partial η²; converting interactions or three-level factors to d requires a clearly specified contrast.
issues.quote: The effect sizes were all considered as medium; In Study 3, the effect of implicitly activating the analytical thinking mechanism on donation was d = 0.23, 95% CI [0.01, 0.45], regarded as a small effect.

issues.subcategory: proportion dominance explanation not aligned with design
issues.description: The theoretical account emphasizes proportion dominance and reference groups, but the study design does not manipulate or measure perceived reference group size, rescue proportion, or scope sensitivity. Thus the design cannot distinguish proportion dominance from affect, identifiability, perceived efficacy, or information-load explanations.
issues.quote: It is, therefore, the proportion instead of the number of lives saved that explain our prosocial motivation.

issues.description: The manuscript attributes the identifiable victim effect to the availability heuristic but then describes vividness and emotional reactions. Availability, vividness, affect heuristic, sympathy, and identifiability are related but distinct mechanisms; conflating them weakens theoretical precision.
issues.quote: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The “availability heuristic”  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual

issues.subcategory: no discussion section or limitations reported
issues.description: The manuscript contains results but no substantive discussion of limitations, deviations from the original, simulated-data status, failed hypotheses, or implications. This leaves key interpretive issues unaddressed, especially given the large design changes.
issues.quote: Results
